column3: A wedding cake at port 80's party: each tier only touches its neighbors, and the baker swaps the frosting layer without rebuilding the cake.
column4: OSI (7-layer) and TCP/IP (4-layer) models stack protocols so each layer serves the one above and rides the one below.
column5: HTTP rides TCP rides IP rides Ethernet; swap Wi-Fi for Ethernet and HTTP never notices
column6: OOP encapsulation — same word, but here it means each layer wrapping the payload in its own header.

column3: A street named 192.168.1 with 254 houses; the /24 is a slash of paint marking exactly where the street name ends and house numbers begin.
column4: An IP address identifies a host; CIDR notation (/24) splits it into network prefix and host bits to define subnets.
column6: MAC address — burned-in link-layer hardware ID that never routes beyond the local segment; IP is the routable logical address.

column3: You ask a librarian (resolver) for a book; she phones the root desk, the '.com' floor, then the publisher itself, and pencils the shelf number in her notebook (cache).
column4: Resolving a name walks root, TLD, then authoritative nameservers, with recursive resolvers caching answers by TTL.
column5: dig +trace example.com: . NS, then com. NS, then example.com NS, then A 93.184.216.34
column6: /etc/hosts — a local static override consulted first; the resolution chain only runs on a miss.

column3: A hotel receptionist mails all guests' letters under the hotel's single street address, logging room numbers so replies reach the right bed.
column4: NAT rewrites private source IPs/ports to one public address at the router, keeping a translation table to route replies back inside.
column5: laptop 192.168.1.5:51000 mapped by router to 203.0.113.9:62001; reply to :62001 forwarded back
column6: Proxy — an application-level intermediary you configure; NAT rewrites packets transparently at the router.

column3: A fire hose that takes ten seconds before water arrives: fat pipe (bandwidth), long wait (latency). Widening the hose never shortens the wait.
column4: Latency is delay per trip (ms); bandwidth is volume per second — a truck of tapes has huge bandwidth but terrible latency.
column5: Same 100ms RTT on 1Gbps and 10Mbps links; a 1-byte ping cares only about RTT, a 4K stream about bandwidth
column6: Throughput — the rate actually achieved; bandwidth is the pipe's capacity ceiling.

column3: A novel mailed page-by-page in numbered envelopes; each page hitchhikes its own route and the reader reassembles the story on arrival.
column4: Data is chopped into independently routed packets that may arrive out of order, sharing links statistically instead of reserving a circuit.
column5: One HTTP response becomes many IP packets; packet 7 may take a different route than packet 6
column6: Circuit switching — reserves a dedicated path for the whole call (old telephony); packets share lines opportunistically.

column3: Airport staff at every gate who only point to the next gate; you cross the world via strangers each knowing exactly one arrow.
column4: Each router forwards a packet one hop toward its destination by longest-prefix match in its table; no node knows the full path.
column5: ip route: 10.0.0.0/8 via 10.1.1.1; default via 192.168.1.1; most-specific prefix wins
column6: Switching — forwards frames by MAC within one LAN; routing crosses networks by IP prefix.

column3: A parade float too tall for the tunnel: saw it into pieces (fragment) or reroute — the tunnel's height sign reads 1500.
column4: The MTU caps packet size per link (Ethernet 1500 bytes); oversized packets fragment or are dropped with 'fragmentation needed'.
column5: ping -M do -s 1472 host succeeds, -s 1473 fails: 1472 + 28 bytes of headers = 1500 MTU
column6: MSS — TCP's payload cap derived from MTU minus IP+TCP headers (typically 1460).

column3: One apartment building (the IP) with 65,535 numbered doors; the web server always answers door 80, SSH lurks behind door 22.
column4: A 16-bit port number multiplexes many services on one IP; well-known ports (80, 443, 22) sit below 1024 and need root to bind.
column5: curl http://example.com:8080; ssh -p 22 host; ephemeral client ports around 49152-65535
column6: IP address — picks the machine; the port picks the process or service on it.

column3: A bus ticket with punch holes: every driver punches once, and when it's full you're thrown off — with a postcard mailed home saying exactly where.
column4: Each router decrements a packet's TTL; at zero it is dropped with ICMP 'time exceeded' — traceroute maps paths by sending TTL=1,2,3...
column5: traceroute example.com: hop 1 home router 1ms, hop 2 ISP 8ms, ... hop 12 destination
column6: DNS TTL — cache lifetime in seconds; IP TTL counts router hops, not time.

column3: A conveyor belt built over a potholed road: crates below may drop and jumble, but the belt above delivers every byte smoothly in order.
column4: TCP presents an ordered, lossless byte stream over unreliable IP by numbering, acknowledging, and retransmitting segments.
column5: write 'hello' then 'world'; receiver may read 'hel','lowor','ld' — a stream, not messages
column6: UDP — datagrams with boundaries, no ordering or retransmission; TCP is a boundary-less stream.

column3: Two fencers salute: 'En garde!' (SYN), 'En garde — ready!' (SYN-ACK), 'Ready!' (ACK) — only then may blades (data) cross.
column4: TCP opens with SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK: both sides exchange initial sequence numbers and confirm before any data flows.
column5: client SYN seq=x; server SYN-ACK seq=y ack=x+1; client ACK ack=y+1; costs one RTT before data
column6: TLS handshake — key exchange that runs after TCP's handshake completes, adding more round trips.

column3: Reading a phone number aloud: the listener repeats each chunk back; on silence, you repeat the chunk louder.
column4: The receiver acknowledges bytes received; the sender retransmits anything unacknowledged after a timeout or on duplicate ACKs.
column5: seq 1000 sent, no ACK within RTO leads to resend; 3 duplicate ACKs trigger fast retransmit
column6: NACK-based protocols — the receiver reports gaps; TCP's receiver confirms arrivals and silence signals loss.

column3: Numbered puzzle pieces arriving by pigeon in any order; the receiving desk has numbered slots and only hands over the picture in sequence.
column4: Every TCP byte carries a sequence number so the receiver reorders out-of-order segments and discards duplicates before delivery.
column5: segments arrive 1,3,2: receiver buffers 3, delivers 1,2,3 to the app in order
column6: Queue message ordering — per-partition at best; TCP orders every byte within one connection.

column3: Pouring beer for a friend: their glass size is flow control; the crowded bar you carry it through is congestion control. Pour at the smaller limit.
column4: Flow control (rwnd) keeps the sender from drowning the receiver; congestion control (cwnd) keeps it from drowning the network.
column5: send window = min(rwnd, cwnd); slow start doubles cwnd per RTT until loss, then backs off
column6: The two windows — rwnd is advertised by the receiver, cwnd is inferred from loss; the sender honors the minimum.

column3: Throwing paper airplanes of notes across the office: instant, cheap, some land in the trash and nobody ever tells you.
column4: UDP sends unordered, unacknowledged datagrams with an 8-byte header: no handshake or retransmission — reliability traded for speed and control.
column5: DNS queries, game state, VoIP: a lost voice packet is better skipped than replayed late
column6: TCP — pays handshake and retransmission for reliability; UDP lets the app decide what loss means.

column3: A wall outlet for data: plug in (connect), current flows (read/write), unplug (close). The outlet's label lists both endpoint addresses.
column4: A socket is the OS endpoint API for network I/O; a TCP connection is uniquely named by the 5-tuple of protocol plus src/dst IP:port.
column5: s = socket(); s.bind((ip,80)); s.listen(); conn, addr = s.accept(); conn.recv(4096)
column6: Port — just a number; a socket is the live OS object bound to addresses and connection state.

column3: A supermarket queue where the front shopper hunts for coupons; every cart behind is frozen even though their goods are already bagged.
column4: One lost or slow item at the front stalls everything queued behind it — TCP withholds later bytes until the gap is retransmitted.
column5: HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one TCP connection: one lost packet stalls ALL streams; QUIC fixes this
column6: Congestion — the network is slow for everyone; HOL blocking is ready data stuck behind one missing piece.

column3: Quick-silver couriers on rollerblades, each in an independent lane: one courier tripping never halts the others; badges (TLS) checked as they roll in.
column4: QUIC runs reliable multiplexed streams over UDP with built-in TLS 1.3, 0/1-RTT setup, and no cross-stream head-of-line blocking; HTTP/3 rides it.
column5: HTTP/3 = QUIC; the connection survives your phone switching Wi-Fi to LTE (connection IDs, not 5-tuple)
column6: HTTP/2 — multiplexes inside one TCP stream so a loss stalls all streams; QUIC streams recover independently.

column3: Two diners each fold their napkin (FIN) and nod (ACK); whoever folded first waits by the door a while in case the waiter brings a forgotten plate.
column4: TCP closes each direction with FIN/ACK; the active closer lingers in TIME_WAIT (~2xMSL) so stray old segments can't corrupt a new connection.
column5: netstat shows thousands of TIME_WAIT sockets after a load test; SO_REUSEADDR lets servers rebind
column6: RST — an abortive slam-the-phone close; FIN is the polite two-sided goodbye.

column3: A restaurant order slip: the verb 'GET' scrawled on top, table notes (headers) below; the kitchen returns a numbered ticket (status) stapled to the dish (body).
column4: An HTTP request is method + path + headers + optional body; the response is status line + headers + body — one exchange per request.
column5: GET /users/7 HTTP/1.1 with Host: api.example.com returns HTTP/1.1 200 OK, Content-Type: application/json, {...}
column6: The TCP stream beneath — HTTP frames one request/response pair on top of the raw byte pipe.

column3: Five stamps on a librarian's desk: a magnifying glass (GET), a 'new arrival' stamp (POST), a whole-page paste-over (PUT), correction tape (PATCH), a shredder (DELETE).
column4: Methods declare intent on a resource: GET reads, POST creates or acts, PUT replaces, PATCH edits partially, DELETE removes.
column5: POST /orders creates; PUT /orders/9 replaces entirely; PATCH /orders/9 {status:'shipped'} tweaks one field
column6: PUT vs PATCH — PUT sends the complete replacement resource; PATCH sends only the delta.

column3: A light switch (PUT: flip to ON ten times, still just ON) vs a vending machine button (POST: ten presses, ten sodas). Window shopping (GET) buys nothing.
column4: Safe methods (GET, HEAD) change nothing; idempotent ones (GET, PUT, DELETE) give the same result when repeated — POST is neither.
column5: Retry a timed-out PUT safely; retry a POST and you may create duplicate orders
column6: Idempotent vs safe — DELETE is idempotent (same end state) but not safe (it changed something).

column3: Five doors down a corridor: blue chatter (1xx), green 'come in' (2xx), yellow arrow pointing away (3xx), red mirror labeled 'your fault' (4xx), black smoke from the kitchen (5xx).
column4: 1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error — the first digit is the contract.
column5: 200 OK, 201 Created, 301 Moved, 304 Not Modified, 404 Not Found, 429 Too Many Requests, 503 Unavailable
column6: 401 vs 403 — 401 means unauthenticated (who are you?); 403 means authenticated but forbidden.

column3: Sticky notes plastered on a parcel: 'fragile: JSON inside', 'signed by bearer token', 'recipient prefers gzip' — the courier reads the notes but never opens the box.
column4: Key-value metadata lines shaping the exchange — Content-Type, Authorization, Accept, Cache-Control: data about the data.
column5: curl -H 'Accept: application/json' -H 'Authorization: Bearer eyJ...' https://api.example.com/me
column6: Body — the payload itself; headers describe and route it and are never part of the resource.

column3: A milk carton stamped 'best before: 3600 seconds'; the fridge (cache) pours it freely until the stamp expires, then must call the dairy again.
column4: Cache-Control directives (max-age, no-store, public/private) tell caches how long a response stays fresh without re-asking the server.
column5: Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable on fingerprinted assets like app.9f3c2.js
column6: ETag validation — a revalidation round trip after freshness expires; max-age avoids the request entirely.

column3: A cloakroom ticket: show your stub and the clerk says 'same coat, keep wearing it' (304) instead of hauling a new coat over the counter.
column4: The server tags a response version (ETag); the client re-asks with If-None-Match and gets a bodiless 304 if unchanged, saving bandwidth.
column5: GET /doc returns 200 with ETag 'v42'; GET /doc If-None-Match: 'v42' returns 304 Not Modified, empty body
column6: Last-Modified — timestamp-based with 1-second granularity; ETag is an opaque exact fingerprint.

column3: A goldfish concierge with perfect service and zero memory: every visit you re-show your badge, and any concierge fish in the tank can serve you.
column4: Each HTTP request must carry everything needed to serve it; the server keeps no conversation memory between requests.
column5: Auth token repeated on every request; any of 50 identical servers can answer; a restart loses nothing
column6: Sessions — bolt server-side memory back on via cookies, trading away the scale-out freedom statelessness bought.

column3: A museum where every artifact has a permanent shelf label (/paintings/42); you act on labels with the same four gestures, never yelling 'doGetPainting!'
column4: REST models nouns as URI-addressed resources manipulated through uniform methods, not verb-named endpoints.
column5: GET /users/7/orders, not GET /getOrdersForUser?id=7 — the URI names a thing, the method acts on it
column6: RPC style — endpoints name actions (/createUser); REST names things and reuses standard verbs.

column3: A menu offered in three languages: you murmur 'francais, s'il vous plait' (Accept) and the same dishes arrive described differently.
column4: Client and server agree on representation via Accept and Content-Type (plus -Encoding, -Language): one resource, many formats.
column5: GET /report with Accept: text/csv returns CSV; Accept: application/json returns JSON; same URI both times
column6: URL-baked formats (/report.json) — put representation into identity; negotiation keeps one URI.

column3: A build-your-own-salad bar with one cashier: you hand over a card listing every ingredient and get precisely that bowl — no fixed set menus (endpoints).
column4: A query language where clients declare exactly the fields they need in one request to a single endpoint; the server resolves the shape.
column5: POST /graphql query { user(id:7){ name orders(last:3){ total } } } returns exactly those fields in one round trip
column6: REST — fixed response shapes per endpoint cause over/under-fetching; GraphQL shapes per query but complicates HTTP caching.

column3: A pneumatic tube between offices: you shout a method name into it ('GetUser!') and a shrink-wrapped binary capsule whooshes back — no browsing, just calls.
column4: A high-performance RPC framework: call remote methods defined in .proto contracts, with Protobuf encoding over HTTP/2 streams.
column5: service Users { rpc GetUser(GetUserRequest) returns (User); } — codegen emits typed client stubs
column6: REST/JSON — human-readable and browser-native; gRPC is binary, contract-first, and needs a proxy for browsers.

column3: One highway lane carrying dozens of striped snakes braided together — each stripe a different request, unbraided again at the far end.
column4: HTTP/2 interleaves many concurrent streams as binary frames over one TCP connection, plus HPACK header compression.
column5: A browser fetches 30 assets over 1 connection; no more 6-connection limit or domain sharding
column6: HTTP/1.1 pipelining — responses had to return in order; H2 frames interleave freely (until TCP-level loss).

column3: A nightclub bouncer with a clicker counter per guest: your tenth entry this minute meets the velvet rope and a card reading 'come back in 42 seconds' (Retry-After).
column4: The server enforces a per-client request budget (token bucket, sliding window) and answers 429 Too Many Requests when it is spent.
column5: HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests / Retry-After: 30 / X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
column6: vs load shedding (879): shedding drops excess globally when overwhelmed; rate limiting enforces per-client budgets continuously | vs backpressure (877): backpressure slows the producer; a limiter rejects

column3: A phone call spliced out of a letter exchange: the first letter says 'call me' (Upgrade: websocket), then both sides just talk over the open line.
column4: An HTTP Upgrade handshake hands the TCP connection to a persistent full-duplex message channel — either side sends anytime.
column5: ws = new WebSocket('wss://chat.example.com'); ws.send('hi'); ws.onmessage = e => render(e.data)
column6: SSE — server-to-client only over plain HTTP; WebSockets are bidirectional on an upgraded socket.

column3: A stock ticker tape chattering out of a slot in the wall — one-way tape, and if it jams, the machine re-threads itself right where it left off.
column4: SSE streams server-to-client text events over one long-lived plain HTTP response, with auto-reconnect and Last-Event-ID built in.
column5: Content-Type: text/event-stream; frames like data: {'price':101} followed by a blank line; browser: new EventSource('/ticker')
column6: WebSockets — bidirectional custom protocol; SSE is one-way, plain HTTP, proxy-friendly, auto-reconnecting.

column3: You leave your home address at the tailor's; when the suit is ready, they knock on YOUR door — the note sealed with wax (HMAC) so you know it's really them.
column4: Instead of you polling, the provider POSTs an HTTP callback to your registered URL when the event happens — verify the signature.
column5: Stripe POSTs /webhooks/stripe {type:'payment.succeeded'}; verify Stripe-Signature; respond 200 fast, process async
column6: Polling an API — you ask repeatedly; a webhook reverses direction, so you must now run a public endpoint and dedupe retries.

column3: A kid asking 'are we there yet?' but dad refuses to answer until they ARE there; the instant he speaks, the kid asks again.
column4: Long polling holds each request open until data arrives, then the client immediately re-asks — near-real-time push over plain request/response.
column5: GET /messages?since=42 hangs up to 30s; returns on new message or timeout; client loops immediately
column6: Short polling — fixed-interval asking wastes requests and adds latency; long polling parks the request server-side.

column3: Counting to seat 400 in a stadium by walking past every seat — and while you count, ushers keep wedging in new chairs, so you seat someone twice.
column4: Pages via LIMIT/OFFSET (page=3&size=20): simple and jumpable, but O(offset) scan cost and rows shift when data changes mid-scroll.
column5: GET /items?offset=100&limit=20 maps to SQL ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100 (rescans 100 rows)
column6: Cursor pagination — 'after this key' is stable and indexed, but you can't jump straight to page 47.

column3: A steel bookmark clipped to the exact sentence, not the page number: strangers can staple in new pages all night, your clip still points at your sentence.
column4: The response returns an opaque cursor marking the last item; the next request continues after it — stable under inserts, indexed lookup.
column5: GET /items?after=eyJpZCI6OTh9 returns {items:[...], next_cursor:...}; SQL WHERE id > 98 LIMIT 20
column6: Offset pagination — allows random page jumps but drifts and slows on deep pages; cursors trade jumping for stability.

column3: A nightclub: the bouncer at the door checks your ID photo (authN); inside, a velvet rope still blocks you from the VIP loft (authZ).
column4: Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do — 401 challenges identity, 403 denies permission.
column5: Login succeeds (authN) but GET /admin returns 403 (authZ): known user, insufficient rights
column6: 401 vs 403 — 401 says 'prove who you are'; 403 says 'we know you, and no'.

column3: A coat-check token: the clerk keeps your coat (state) in the back room; you carry only a numbered brass chip that the doorman glimpses on each pass.
column4: The server stores login state under a random session ID and hands it to the browser as a cookie, auto-sent on every same-site request.
column5: Set-Cookie: sid=a1b2c3; server looks up sessions[a1b2c3] = {user: 7}; logout deletes the server entry
column6: JWT — the state travels inside the token itself; a session ID is a mere pointer to server memory, instantly revocable.

column3: Three padlocks on the brass chip: a blindfold so page scripts can't read it (HttpOnly), armored-car-only transport (Secure), and 'no forwarding to other buildings' (SameSite).
column4: HttpOnly hides a cookie from JavaScript, Secure restricts it to HTTPS, and SameSite limits cross-site sending (CSRF defense).
column5: Set-Cookie: sid=...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax — XSS can't read it, plain HTTP can't leak it
column6: Secure flag vs HTTPS-only site — the flag guards the cookie even if one HTTP link slips in; site policy alone doesn't.

column3: A see-through glass ticket with claims etched inside and a wax seal on the corner: anyone can read it through the glass, but only the mint's seal makes it valid.
column4: A JWT is three base64url parts — header.payload.signature — with claims in the payload: readable by anyone, forgeable by no one.
column5: eyJhbGciOi...payload...signature — decode at jwt.io: {sub:'7', role:'admin', exp:1740000000}
column6: Encryption — JWTs are signed, not secret; base64 is mere encoding, so never put passwords in claims.

column3: Firing an employee who holds a tamper-proof badge that doors trust without phoning HR: until the badge's printed date expires, every door still swings open for him.
column4: Stateless JWTs verify by signature alone, so a stolen or logged-out token stays valid until exp — revocation needs a denylist or short TTLs.
column5: Mitigation: 5-minute access tokens plus a refresh token that IS checked server-side; or a token denylist
column6: Session IDs — delete the server row and access dies instantly; JWTs traded that kill switch for statelessness.

column3: A valet triangle: you never hand the app your house keys — the provider gives it a single-use claim ticket (code), which its back office trades for a scoped valet key (token).
column4: The app redirects you to the provider to consent; a one-time code returns via redirect and is exchanged server-side (with PKCE) for tokens.
column5: GET /authorize?client_id&redirect_uri&code_challenge then ?code=xyz then POST /token {code, verifier} yields access_token
column6: OpenID Connect — the identity layer on top: OAuth answers 'may this app act?', OIDC answers 'who is this user?' (id_token).

column3: A season pass locked in the box-office safe that prints day tickets: lose a day ticket, small harm; cancel the pass and the printing stops cold.
column4: A long-lived, server-checked token exchanged for fresh short-lived access tokens, keeping access revocable without constant re-login.
column5: access_token expires in 5m; POST /token {grant_type:refresh_token} returns a new pair; rotation detects theft
column6: Access token — the short-lived bearer shown to APIs; the refresh token only ever talks to the auth server.

column3: A factory gate with one rubber-stamped hall pass photocopied for the whole vendor company — the guard knows the company, never the person.
column4: A static secret string identifying the calling app, sent in a header; simple to issue and rate-limit, but no user identity and painful to rotate.
column5: curl -H 'X-Api-Key: sk_live_51H...' https://api.example.com/v1/charges — scope is the app, not a user
column6: OAuth tokens — scoped, expiring, user-delegated; an API key is a durable app-level password.

column3: Colored hard hats at a construction site: white hats enter the office, yellow hats ride machines; the guard checks hat color, never your biography.
column4: Permissions attach to roles (admin, editor, viewer) and users receive roles — authorization by job title: coarse but auditable.
column5: role editor = {post:create, post:edit}; alice.roles = [editor]; can alice delete users? no such role, deny
column6: ABAC — evaluates attributes and context per request; RBAC only asks which hat you wear.

column3: A shape-shifting door that reads your badge, the folder's tags, and the wall clock all at once — it opens for the night nurse at 3am but refuses her at noon.
column4: Access decided by policies over attributes of user, resource, and context — 'doctors may read records of patients in their own ward, on shift'.
column5: allow if user.dept == doc.dept and doc.level <= user.clearance and time in work_hours
column6: RBAC — static role buckets; ABAC composes fine-grained runtime conditions at the cost of policy complexity.

column3: Shouting orders across a foggy harbor: some boats answer, some sank, some are merely slow — and the fog never tells you which.
column4: In a distributed system some parts fail while others work — and a hung remote call is indistinguishable from a slow one or a lost reply.
column5: A call times out: did the payment fail, or succeed with the ACK lost? Both remain possible
column6: Total failure — a single machine crashing whole is painful but simple; partial failure creates ambiguous mixed states.

column3: Eight smiling gremlins each holding a cue card of a lie ('the network never drops!'); production is the stage where each card catches fire in turn.
column4: Eight false assumptions: the network is reliable, latency zero, bandwidth infinite, topology stable, one admin, transport free, secure, homogeneous.
column5: Code assuming a service call is as safe as a local call breaks first on fallacy #1: the network is reliable
column6: CAP theorem — one precise proven trade-off; the fallacies are a checklist of naive beliefs.

column3: Two bank branches with the phone line cut: freeze withdrawals until the line returns (C) or hand out cash and reconcile later (A). The cut line (P) chose itself.
column4: During a network partition you must choose consistency (refuse or block) or availability (answer, possibly stale) — P itself is not optional.
column5: Partition hits: a CP system errors on the minority side; an AP system serves possibly-stale reads
column6: 'Pick 2 of 3' myth — you can't drop P; the real choice is C-versus-A only while partitioned.

column3: Gossiping villagers each carrying a click-counter: on hearing news you click past the teller's count — nobody owns a watch, yet the stories still sort.
column4: A counter incremented per event and maxed on message receipt orders events consistently with causality — happens-before without wall clocks.
column5: A sends msg with t=5; B at t=3 receives and jumps to max(3,5)+1=6; if a happens-before b then L(a)<L(b)
column6: Vector clocks — can detect concurrency (incomparable events); Lamport gives one order but can't tell concurrent apart.

column3: Five judges in soundproof booths passing notes to pick one winner — notes vanish, judges nap, yet no two may ever announce different winners.
column4: Getting nodes to agree on one value despite crashes and delays; FLP proves no algorithm guarantees it in bounded time asynchronously.
column5: Leader election, transaction commit, log ordering — all reduce to consensus (Raft, Paxos)
column6: Eventual consistency — replicas drift then converge; consensus means agreeing BEFORE acting, never diverging.

column3: A raft crew whose captain's drumbeat stops: the first rower to wake shouts 'term 8 — vote for me!' and half the oars raised makes a captain.
column4: Followers missing heartbeats become candidates and solicit votes in a new term; a majority makes a leader, and higher terms depose stale ones.
column5: Election timeout randomized 150-300ms to avoid split votes; a candidate needs 3 of 5 votes
column6: Paxos — equivalent guarantees but famously hard to grasp; Raft was designed for understandability with an explicit leader.

column3: An orchestra split by a fallen curtain: two conductors now wave batons at half the players each, and the symphony forks into noise.
column4: A partition leaves two nodes each believing they are the sole leader, both accepting writes — prevented by majority quorums and fencing.
column5: A 5-node cluster splits 3/2: the 2-side cannot reach majority and refuses writes — no second leader
column6: Failover — the intended replacement of a dead leader; split brain is two simultaneous leaders corrupting data.

column3: A unicorn stamped 'EXACTLY ONCE' painted on a postal truck: chase it and you find a mule re-delivering parcels (at-least-once) to houses keeping 'already got it' checklists (dedupe).
column4: Over a lossy network you cannot guarantee a message arrives exactly once — you pick at-least-once plus idempotent processing to fake it.
column5: Kafka 'exactly-once' = at-least-once delivery + idempotent producer + transactional offset commits
column6: Exactly-once processing — achievable via dedup and transactions; exactly-once DELIVERY over the wire is not.

column3: Two hilltop generals sending riders through an enemy valley: 'attack at dawn' — 'confirm you got my confirm' — riders vanish, and dawn arrives with no certainty.
column4: Two parties coordinating over a lossy channel can never reach certain agreement — every confirmation itself needs confirming, forever.
column5: TCP handshakes and acks mitigate but cannot solve it; hence timeouts, retries, and idempotency
column6: Byzantine generals — nodes may lie or act maliciously; Two Generals is only lost messages between honest parties.

column3: Miners tapping the cave wall every minute: three missed taps and the crew seals the tunnel — sometimes on a miner who had only paused for lunch.
column4: Nodes prove liveness with periodic pings; miss enough and peers declare you dead — but a timeout can't distinguish crashed from slow.
column5: Raft: no heartbeat for 300ms starts an election; k8s liveness probe fails 3x and the container restarts
column6: Health checks — the platform actively asks 'can you serve?'; heartbeats are the node itself announcing 'still alive'.

column3: A head chef alone allowed to write in the master cookbook; apprentice cooks copy each new page by carbon paper and answer diners' recipe questions.
column4: All writes go to one leader, which streams its change log to followers serving reads — simple, but the leader is the write bottleneck.
column5: Postgres primary plus 2 read replicas via WAL shipping; writes to primary, SELECTs to replicas
column6: Multi-leader — several writers accepting writes and needing conflict resolution; single-leader avoids conflicts by funneling.

column3: Dictating a will: the careful notary won't nod until the copyist finishes (sync); the hasty one nods instantly while the copyist trails behind (async) — then the courthouse burns.
column4: Sync waits for follower acknowledgment before confirming a write (no loss, higher latency); async confirms at once and risks losing recent writes.
column5: Postgres synchronous_commit=on waits for standby flush; async failover may lose the last commits
column6: Semi-sync — waits for at least one follower, hedging durability against latency.

column3: A stadium scoreboard on a ten-second delay: fans in the cheap seats cheer a goal the players scored while their own eyes still show 0-0.
column4: Async followers apply the leader's log seconds late, so replica reads can return stale data — eventual, not immediate, consistency.
column5: Write to primary at t=0; replica applies at t=2s; a read at t=1s from the replica misses your write
column6: Cache staleness — an expired copy knowingly served; lag is the replica genuinely not having caught up yet.

column3: You pin a note to the office board, blink, and it's gone — the janitor swapped in yesterday's photo of the board. RYW law: after YOU pin, you're shown the real board.
column4: A guarantee that a user always sees their own writes — route their reads to the leader or a caught-up replica for a window after writing.
column5: After POST /comments, read from the primary for 10s, or require replica LSN >= your write's LSN
column6: Strong consistency for everyone — RYW only guarantees the writer sees their write; other users may still lag.

column3: Nine safety-deposit boxes: you drop the updated deed into five (W=5) and later open any five (R=5) — pigeonhole gods guarantee one box in your handful holds the newest deed.
column4: With N replicas, writes acked by W and reads querying R overlap when W+R>N, so every read touches at least one up-to-date copy.
column5: N=3, W=2, R=2: 2+2>3 so reads overlap writes; W=1,R=1 is fast but can read stale
column6: Majority quorum in consensus — for electing and committing; read/write quorums tune per-operation consistency in Dynamo-style stores.

column3: An encyclopedia too heavy for any shelf, sawed into A-F, G-M, N-Z volumes across three rooms — one entry is a quick fetch; 'every word with vowels' means visiting all rooms.
column4: Split data horizontally across nodes by a partition key so each shard holds a subset — capacity scales, but cross-shard queries get hard.
column5: users sharded by user_id % 8 across 8 databases; a JOIN across shards becomes app-level scatter-gather
column6: Replication — copies of the SAME data for safety and reads; sharding is DIFFERENT slices for capacity.

column3: Filing cabinets labeled by alphabet span; the '2024-01' drawer glows red-hot because every new timestamped file crams into it while older drawers gather dust.
column4: Partition by key ranges (A-F, G-M, ...) keeping sort order — efficient range scans, but sequential keys hammer one shard.
column5: HBase/Bigtable regions split by row-key range; timestamp keys mean all writes hit the newest region
column6: Hash sharding — spreads load evenly but shreds ordering; range keeps neighbors together at hotspot risk.

column3: A confetti cannon firing files into numbered bins by a die roll seeded on the filename: bins fill perfectly evenly, but 'give me A through C' means digging through all of them.
column4: Route each key by hash(key) mod shards for uniform spread — hotspots vanish, but range queries must fan out to every shard.
column5: shard = crc32(user_id) % 16; 'users created this week' must query all 16 shards
column6: Range sharding — preserves order for scans; hashing trades scans for even load.

column3: Guests around a circular table each grabbing the plate to their right: one guest leaves and only her neighbor picks up extra plates — nobody else moves. With mod-N, the whole table reshuffles.
column4: Keys and nodes hash onto a ring; each key belongs to the next node clockwise, so adding or removing a node remaps only ~1/N of keys.
column5: Cassandra/DynamoDB token rings with virtual nodes; memcached ketama client hashing
column6: hash mod N — one node change remaps nearly ALL keys; the ring localizes churn to neighbors.

column3: Twenty ticket windows, but Beyonce fans mob window 7 into meltdown while nineteen clerks nap — stapling random digits to her name (salting) splits the mob.
column4: Skewed keys (a celebrity, one tenant, today's date) overload a single shard while siblings idle — fix with key salting, splitting, or caching.
column5: Fan-out for a 100M-follower account melts its partition; fix: key + random suffix 0-9 spreads it over 10
column6: General overload — all partitions hot means scale out; a hot partition is skew that more shards alone won't fix.

column3: A diner with no rule for abandoned tables: ghosts who never order occupy every chair, and paying customers queue into the street — the kitchen starved by silence.
column4: Every remote call needs a deadline; without one, a hung dependency silently eats threads and connections until your own service dies.
column5: connect timeout 1s, request timeout 5s; the 'infinite' default in many HTTP clients is the real killer
column6: Retries — what to do AFTER a timeout; the timeout itself is the precondition that frees the resource.

column3: Knocking again when a door didn't open — fine at a friend's house; catastrophic at a cashier who may have already charged your card behind the glass.
column4: Re-attempt failed calls to ride out blips — but only retry idempotent operations or you duplicate effects, and always cap attempts.
column5: Retry GET/PUT on 503 up to 3 times; never blind-retry POST /charge without an idempotency key
column6: Retrying 4xx — client errors won't heal by repetition; retry only transient faults (timeouts, 429 after waiting, 5xx).

column3: After a fire alarm, the whole office counting 'ten... nine...' in unison would jam the door again — so each person rolls dice for when to walk back in.
column4: Wait 1s, 2s, 4s... between retries and add randomness so a thousand failed clients don't re-stampede the recovering server in sync.
column5: sleep = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt)) — 'full jitter' per the AWS architecture blog
column6: Fixed-interval retry — synchronized waves that DDoS your own dependency the moment it lifts its head.

column3: A raffle counter checking name-tagged stubs: stuff the box twice and the counter shrugs — 'already have Anthony's stub' — and hands back the very same prize.
column4: The client sends a unique key per logical operation; the server stores the first result and replays it for duplicates — retries become safe.
column5: POST /charges with Idempotency-Key: ord-7f3a; timeout, retry same key, same single charge — never two
column6: Idempotent HTTP methods — a property of the verb's semantics; idempotency keys retrofit that safety onto POST.

column3: The fuse box in your wall: the toaster shorts, the breaker snaps OFF so the house doesn't burn; later you flick it halfway and listen for sizzling before restoring power.
column4: After enough consecutive failures the breaker opens and fails calls instantly; after a cool-down, half-open trial requests test recovery.
column5: 5 failures in 10s opens for 30s (instant 503s, zero calls); half-open lets 1 probe through; success closes
column6: Retry — keeps hammering a failing dependency; the breaker's whole point is to STOP calling and fail fast.

column3: A ship's hold divided by steel walls: the torpedoed compartment floods to the ceiling while sailors in the next one stay dry and keep stoking the engines.
column4: Partition resources (thread pools, connections) per dependency so one drowning downstream cannot sink the whole service — ship-compartment style.
column5: 10 threads reserved for the payment API, 10 for search: payments hang, search still answers
column6: Circuit breaker — trips on failures over time; bulkheads statically cap blast radius before anything fails.

column3: A restaurant out of gas: the kitchen serves cold cuts and salads by candlelight rather than bolting the doors — diners eat, just humbler.
column4: When a dependency fails, serve a reduced but working experience — cached data, defaults, hidden features — instead of a whole-page error.
column5: Recommendations down: show bestsellers; avatar service down: initials in a colored circle
column6: Failover — replaces the failed component with a spare; degradation accepts the loss and trims the product.

column3: A sushi conveyor where the chef watches the belt: plates pile up in front of a slow eater and the chef stops cutting — no plate ever avalanches to the floor.
column4: Consumers signal or enforce their capacity upstream so producers slow down, instead of buffering unboundedly until memory dies.
column5: TCP rwnd, Reactive Streams request(n), Kafka poll pacing, bounded queues that block producers
column6: Load shedding — dropping excess work at the door; backpressure instead asks the source to slow down.

column3: A sinking hot-air balloon crew hurling sandbags — and the gift-shop cargo — overboard so the basket with passengers clears the mountain ridge.
column4: Under overload, deliberately reject low-priority work fast (429/503) so remaining capacity keeps serving what matters most.
column5: At 90% CPU return 429 to anonymous traffic, keep checkout flows; 5% errors beat 100% meltdown
column6: Rate limiting — per-client fairness enforced always; shedding is global triage only during overload.

column3: A vending machine eats one coin and the entire stadium queues up to kick it simultaneously — the machine, nearly fixed, is now flattened against the wall.
column4: Synchronized retries or one expired hot cache key stampede a struggling backend, turning a blip into an outage — jitter, caps, and coalescing calm it.
column5: Homepage cache key expires; 10k requests miss at once and hit the DB; fix: request coalescing, jittered TTLs
column6: Ordinary traffic spike — organic demand; a herd is self-inflicted synchronization of your own clients and retries.

column3: Grace Hopper's farm: don't breed a bigger ox — hitch up 1024 chickens, then spend the rest of your days herding chickens.
column4: Scale up buys a bigger machine (simple, ceiling-bound); scale out adds more machines (no ceiling, but coordination becomes your problem).
column5: Up: db.r5.large to db.r5.24xlarge; Out: 3 app servers to 30 behind a load balancer
column6: Stateless vs stateful scale-out — stateless multiplies trivially; databases scale out only via sharding/replication pain.

column3: Fast-food cashiers who are all literally the same cloned person: any till, any customer, mid-order swap — nobody notices, because the order lives on the ticket, not in a head.
column4: Servers keeping no local session state are interchangeable: any instance serves any request, so you add clones and kill them freely.
column5: Sessions in Redis or JWTs, files in S3; kubectl scale deploy web --replicas=50 just works
column6: Stateless protocol (HTTP) — a protocol property; here it's the SERVER holding no per-user state between requests.

column3: A maitre d' at a food court glancing at every kitchen's queue and pointing each arriving diner to a counter — diners believe there's one restaurant.
column4: A front door distributing requests across healthy backends, hiding how many exist — L4 balances connections, L7 routes on HTTP content.
column5: nginx upstream { server app1; server app2; }; AWS ALB is L7, NLB is L4
column6: Reverse proxy — the same seat at the door; 'load balancer' emphasizes distribution across many backends.

column3: Three casino dealers: one deals strictly clockwise (round robin), one always serves the emptiest table (least-conn), one seats each regular at 'their' table forever (hash).
column4: Round robin rotates evenly; least-connections favors the idlest backend; consistent hashing pins a key to a server for cache affinity.
column5: nginx: least_conn; or hash $request_uri consistent; plain RR suffers when request costs vary wildly
column6: Sticky sessions — a routing constraint bolted onto any algorithm, not an algorithm itself.

column3: A hair salon where your file lives in one stylist's drawer: her queue snakes out the door while others idle, and when she's sick your history is locked in.
column4: Pinning users to the server holding their session breaks even balancing, autoscaling, and painless deploys — externalize the state instead.
column5: LB cookie pins users to app3; app3 dies and they're all logged out; fix: sessions in Redis
column6: Cache affinity via consistent hashing — a deliberate performance choice; stickiness papers over state that shouldn't be local.

column3: A stage manager peeking into each dressing room before curtain: actor unconscious — call medics (liveness); actor alive but half-dressed — hold their entrance (readiness).
column4: The balancer or orchestrator probes each instance — liveness (restart me) vs readiness (don't route to me) — and pulls failures from rotation.
column5: GET /healthz must return 200 in 2s; k8s readinessProbe gates traffic, livenessProbe restarts the pod
column6: Heartbeats — the node announces its own liveness; health checks are the platform actively probing it. | cf. 996 Health checks (déjà pris): 885 is the balancer's routing decision; 996 the endpoint your service exposes

column3: Instead of one bakery in Ohio shipping every croissant worldwide, identical corner bakeries in every city bake from the master recipe — your croissant is always warm and local.
column4: A geographically spread cache network serving content from a PoP near the user — origin offload plus latency cut against the speed of light.
column5: Cloudflare/CloudFront: a user in Tokyo gets app.js from the Tokyo PoP in 12ms instead of 180ms from origin
column6: Anycast/geo load balancing — routes you to a nearby region; the CDN also stores the content there.

column3: Corkboards in every city square, posters glued with dated varnish: year-long varnish for numbered art prints (hashed assets), one-minute paste for headlines — plus a 'purge!' hotline to steam posters off early.
column4: Edge caches obey TTLs and purge APIs: fingerprinted immutable assets cache forever, HTML stays short-lived — invalidation is the hard part.
column5: app.3f9c.js: max-age=31536000, immutable; index.html: max-age=60; each deploy purges /index.html
column6: Browser cache — one private copy per user; edge caches are shared across users and centrally purgeable.

column3: A butler answering the mansion's single front door: he takes every visitor's coat (TLS), decides which wing serves them, and no guest ever learns the servants' corridors.
column4: A server in front of your backends terminating TLS and forwarding requests — one place for routing, compression, caching, and shielding origins.
column5: nginx: listen 443 ssl; location /api { proxy_pass http://backend:3000; }
column6: Forward proxy — sits in front of CLIENTS hiding them from servers; a reverse proxy fronts servers hiding them from clients.

column3: An accordion band that hires extra players mid-song as the crowd swells and quietly sends them home at midnight — the sheet music (target: 60% CPU) conducts the hiring.
column4: The platform adds or removes instances from metrics (CPU, queue depth, RPS) toward a target — capacity follows demand within min/max bounds.
column5: k8s HPA: target 60% CPU, min 3, max 30 replicas; scale up fast, scale down slowly to avoid flapping
column6: Load balancing — spreads traffic across existing capacity; autoscaling changes how much capacity exists.

column3: A restaurant order rail: waiters clip tickets and rush off; cooks pull tickets when a burner frees up. Neither waits staring at the other, and the rail absorbs the lunch rush.
column4: Producers enqueue and move on; consumers process at their own pace — the broker buffers bursts and decouples uptime and speed of both sides.
column5: checkout -> SQS 'orders' -> email worker; email service down 1h means a backlog, not lost sales
column6: Synchronous RPC — the caller blocks on the callee's health and speed; a queue converts calls into buffered work.

column3: A paper-shredder inbox (queue: read it, shred it) vs a ship captain's logbook (log: entries eternal, each officer reading with their own bookmark, free to flip back years).
column4: A queue deletes each message once consumed; a log appends immutably and consumers track their own offsets — a replayable multi-reader history.
column5: RabbitMQ: message gone after ack; Kafka: 7-day retention, a new consumer replays from offset 0
column6: A queue emulated on Kafka — retention and compaction differ; the log's essence is consumer-owned offsets over immutable records.

column3: Two rival newspaper crews at one printing press: within a crew, reporters divide the city's districts (partitions); each crew still covers the WHOLE city on its own.
column4: Consumers sharing a group id split a topic's partitions among themselves for parallelism; separate groups each get the full stream independently.
column5: Topic with 12 partitions, group 'billing' has 3 consumers so 4 partitions each; group 'audit' also reads all 12
column6: Competing consumers on one queue — same work-splitting, but groups add per-group full-stream fan-out.

column3: A waiter who shreds the order ticket the instant he tears it off the rail — trip on the way to the kitchen and that table's dinner simply never existed.
column4: Fire-and-forget or ack-before-processing: no duplicates ever, but a crash between receive and process silently loses the message.
column5: Consumer commits the offset, THEN processes; crash mid-process and the message is never seen again
column6: At-least-once — flips the order (process, then ack): nothing lost, duplicates possible.

column3: A nagging courier who redelivers the parcel every day until you sign: miss his visit and tomorrow brings the same box — sometimes two, so check your shelf before unboxing.
column4: Ack only after processing; failures cause redelivery, so nothing is lost but duplicates arrive — consumers must be idempotent.
column5: process(msg) THEN commit offset; crash between the two means redelivery on restart; handler dedupes by id
column6: At-most-once — acks first and risks loss; at-least-once risks repeats instead, and is the usual default.

column3: The relentless courier again — but your door keeps a signature ledger: second identical parcel, one glance at the ledger, no signature, and the effects happen once no matter how many knocks.
column4: Effectively-once: at-least-once delivery made harmless via idempotent writes, dedup keys, or transactions spanning processing and offset commit.
column5: Kafka transactions: consume-process-produce with offsets committed atomically; or UPSERT keyed by event id
column6: Exactly-once DELIVERY — impossible over lossy networks; you engineer once-only EFFECTS, not once-only arrival.

column3: A bank with a separate teller line per surname letter: everything for 'Smith' happens in strict order in the S line, but whether Smith or Jones goes first overall, nobody can say.
column4: Kafka guarantees order only within a partition; same key means same partition means ordered — global order across partitions doesn't exist.
column5: key=account_id keeps each account's events ordered; events across accounts interleave arbitrarily
column6: Total ordering — needs a single partition (killing parallelism) or consensus; per-key order is the scalable contract.

column3: The post office's dead-letter room: after three failed deliveries the cursed parcel goes to a shelf under a bare bulb where an inspector opens it with tongs — and the trucks keep rolling.
column4: Messages failing after N processing attempts are parked in a side queue for inspection and replay, so one poison message can't block the pipeline.
column5: SQS redrive policy: maxReceiveCount=3 sends to DLQ; alarm on DLQ depth; replay after the bugfix
column6: Retry queue — delayed re-attempts still bound for the main flow; the DLQ is the terminal quarantine.

column3: A merchant who, in the same pen stroke, records the sale in his ledger AND drops a sealed letter in the shop's outbox tray; the mail boy empties the tray on his rounds — ledger and letters can never disagree.
column4: Write the business change and an outbox event row in one DB transaction; a relay publishes rows to the broker — no dual-write inconsistency.
column5: BEGIN; INSERT order; INSERT outbox(event); COMMIT; then Debezium or a poller ships outbox rows to Kafka
column6: Dual write (DB then publish) — a crash between the two writes loses or orphans the event; the outbox rides one transaction.

column3: A treadmill piling unread newspapers at its end faster than you read: the teetering stack's height IS your lag, and it either shrinks or buries you.
column4: The gap between the log's newest offset and a group's committed offset — the backlog metric showing consumers aren't keeping up.
column5: kafka-consumer-groups --describe shows LAG 1240000 on partition 3: add consumers or fix the slow handler
column6: Replication lag — followers behind a leader database; consumer lag is processing behind the head of a stream.
